NEW YORK, May 27. - Ruth
Brown Snyder's execution,
scheduled for the week of June
20, was automatically stayed
until fall when notice for an
appeal of her -CTJWr !'WKB ' filed
today in Queen County Court.
Gray to Appeal Soon
Mrs. Snyder and her former
lover, Henry Judd Gray, are now
in the deathhouse in Sing Sing
awaiting execution in the electric
chair for the murder of Albert
Snyder.
Gray's appeal will not be filed
for about two weeks.

Grounds for Mrs. Snyder's
appeal .tor a new trial were not
contained in the notice filed this
morning. These will be given in
briefs to be submitted to the court
of appeals by her attorneys.
District Attorney Richard S.
Newcombe also will submit briefs.
Mrs. Snyder, it wag learned, will
sign over her rights to her
husband's insurance of $102,000 to her
nine-year-old daughter, I.orraine.
Mrs. Snyder remains the beneficiary
until the court of appeals passes
on her fate.
Fight for the custody of
Lorraine is to be opened next
Tuesday in a court battle between Mrs.

Josephine Brown, mother of Mrs.
Snyder, and W -.rren Schneider,
brother of the slain man, both of
whom want the child.
Mrs. Snyder is reported In
advices from Sing Sing to be in a
most disheartened mood. For hours
she sits on her cot. staring straight
ahead and speaking to no one.
She has declined to read the
newspapers, saying they make her sad.
Her appetite is poor and she sleeps
fitfully.
Gray, on the other hand, is
taking his plight philosophically. He
even smiled when death house
attaches told him a Baltimore woman
claimed she was his wife, that he
was a bigamist.

"That's absurd," Gray smiled.
"Why worry anyway - haven't I
enough troubles?"

Associated Press of Lindbergh's start eight

calling together various persons

France. There may be some fog, says

report, hut the probabilities are that he

wind - regarded as most, favorable -

the Gulf of St. Lawrence. High
pressure areas known technically as
"anti! cyclones" extend over the Atlantic as
far as Ireland.

north, however, for low pressure will
prevail during the morning in the
region directly south of Greenland and
southwest of Ireland.

compass. sitting in an inclosed cockpit,
evokes astonishment, and all the
commentators express admiration for his
courage.

Mrs. Elzina Thornton, 75,

Unable because of her advanced

hospital where Dr. Purney attended
her. She was resting comfortably at

rleath was not expected. She was
burned about the face, hands, and
upper part of her body.

education in that place. About seven years

husband, who died on March 4. Had
the couple lived until the early part
of next month they would have
celebrated their 62nd wedding
anniversary. Mrs. Thornton was a member of
St. Marks Episcopal church.

grandchild ren.

o'clock. The remains will be taken

there.

Moderator Delivers Sermon

HI Dorado, Ark., May l'J. - (/P) -
Dr. R. F. Campbell of Asheville,
N. C" was elected moderator of
the general assembly, of the
Presbyterian Church in the United
States here late today on the first
ballot. Others nominated were
Dr. Ernest Thompson, Charleston,
W. Va.; Dr. Charles R. Nesbit,
Kansas City, Mo., and I)r. K. T.
VVellford, Newport News, Va.
The ti7th annual meeting of the
church began here this morning
when the sermon by Dr. J. \V.
Skinner, retiring moderator, was
delivered. Doctor Skinner, who is
president of the Texas-Mexican
Industrial Institute for Boys at
Kingsville, Texas, praised
scientists as agroup of men who have
done great things to advance the
happiness of the human race.

Radical changes in the
machinery of the church are proposed in
the report of the committee on
survey, regarded as one of the most
important business matters to
come before the assembly, wlfcich
is expected to be given
consideration tomorrow. The report
recommends that the executive and
promotional agencies of the church
between meetings of the general
assembly be supervised by a
committee of 44, including 11 women.
Referring to natural and
political disorders of the past year
in the southern part of this
country, in Mexico and in China,
Doctor Skinner declared that the
church has experienced a year of
peace. "No doctrinal nor
ecclesiastical typhoon has made havoc
'in our midst,'' he said.

"God is known as a greater god
today than was taught 200 years
ago," the moderator said in his
sermon. "The Bible is a richer
treasure of truth in the light of the
illumination of modern science.
No class of men live and labor more
in the spirit of Jesus Christ than
self-effacing, men of scienr_
tific research laboratories."
"Doctor Skinner credited the
scientists with having "done more
in the last few years to make the
world safe for a new race of men,
more to make available more
favorable conditions for men, more to
take fear out of the hearts of men,
more to take the drudgery out of
human toil, more to banish
ignorance, more to bring in light than
the church of God did for 1,000
years in the centuries between
400 and 1400."

departments of the church's affairs

were in good shape and have held

WILL CONTINUE
FIGHT IN COURT
Twice Convicted of Murder
Greenville Man Asks For
New Trial and Will
Appeal to Supreme Court
Greenville, May 10. - UP) - A
motion for a new trial for Jerry
Hester. who was convicted of murder
with recommendation to mercy this
morning for the slaying of J. Ed
Thaekston, on the night of
December 20, 1024, will be argued before
Judge T. J. Mauldin tomorrow
afternoon, it was staled tonight by
J. D. Hanford, one of his attorneys.
The same jury that convicted
Jerry acquitted liis two sons,
Charlie and Claude. All three
defendants were convicted at the first
trial, held a few' weeks after the
slaying. The supreme court
ordered the second hearing.

In case the new trial move fails,
the defense is expected to note its
intention to appeal. Also, if the
new trial move is not carried, Jerry
will be formally sentenced
tomorrow afternoon. His conviction with
the recommendation to mercy
automatically calls for a life
imprisonment sentence. He is now 59
years of age.
In case the new trial is granted
or in case an appeal is taken, the
defense will in all probability move
before an associate justice for bail
for the convicted man, it was
indicated by Mr. Lanford. Hester
has been in prison 29 months since
the ease arose.

One of the strong grounds to
which the defense is looking for
an appeal foundation, if one is
necessary, is the refusal of Judge
Mauldin to quash the venire drawn
for the week of the trial. The
move was based on the grounds
that J. Ben Watkins, county
auditor and hence a member of the
jury commission, is a
brother-inlaw of one of Trackston's
daughters.
Charlie and Claude Hester, the
acquitted sons, walked out of the
court room free men following
nearly 30 months of accusation,
about half of that time being spent.,
under sentence of death. They are
looking for work, their counsel
stated. Jerry, the father, is more
hopeful for his ultimate freedom
than at any time since his arrest.

AVIATOR ROYALLY ENTERTAINED BY FRENCH
I aris, May 21. - Capt. Charles A. Lindbergh, the young
American aviator, who hopped off from New York Friday morning all
alone in his monoplane, arrived in Paris Saturday night, safe and
sound, as everyone hoped he had.

The sandy-haired son of the middle west dropped down out of
the darkness at Le Bourget flying field, a few miles from Paris,
at 10:21 o clock Saturday night (5:21 p. m. New York time) only
331/2 hours after leaving Long Island - the first man in history to
go from New York to Paris without changing his seat.
io the young American it was seemingly merely the
achievement oi an ambition. To Paris, to France, to America, to the
moi Id, his landing Saturday night made him the greatest of
heioes mankind has produced since the air became a means of
travel.

25,000 Surround Plane
A crowd of at least 25,000
surrounded his plane, the "Spirit of St.
Louis," when it came to earth after
its epochal voyage from the New
World to the Old. The airman lifted
from the seat, where for two days
and a night he sat fixed, guiding his
plane over land and sea, and for
minutes he was hardly able to talk
or do anything else, except let
himself be carried along by a mass
men made delirious with joy at his
achievement.

Greatest Welcome Ever.
Never has an aviator of any nation,
even king or ruler, had a greater
more spontaneous welcome from the
hearts of the •common people
France. The very recklessness of his
endeavor, as it appeared, appealed
the quick emotional imagination
Frenchmen, and they were quick
respond with everything their own
hearts could give.
All ties of nationalism were
forgotten by the Le Bourget throng. They
saw in Lindbergh only a man who had
brilliantly gambled with death and

Point, May 23. - Ferdinand
Schlaps, who was hanged May 20 for
the murder of Mr, and Mrs. Tony
Geisler on May 1 , 1926, was buried

afternoon. His mother, Christina
Schlaps, and all of his brothers and
sisters were present, as well as some

Service were conducted by Mr. and

It was a dismal day. A drizzlng

gathered at the Coliseum where services
were held. Saturday many people
viewed the body at the undertaking
parlor.
Schlaps Pays the Price
Wolf Point. - Ferdinand
was brought to the scaffold and
hanged at midnight last Thursday
before a great crowd of curiosity
seekers who were invited by Sheriff
Anderson to witness the gruesome
deed. The crowd, with craned necks,
viewed the death march of the
condemned man to the Gallows,
there Sheriff Anderson, who acted as
hangman, assisted by Deputy Sheriff
Council, performed the task
expeditiously if a bit nervously. Schlaps
seemed to be the most unconcerned
man in the crowd. When he mounted
the scaffold he was heard to say
"Goodbye world. Oh Jesus." Schlaps
was of a deeply religious nature
having been brought up by German
Lutheran parents and being a regular

church goer until he went to work
for the Geislers and then when he
could get an opportunity to go. He
was a constant reader of the Bible in
his cell and his deep religious faith
that he was going to a better place is
believed by many to have caused his
stoical indifference to death at the
end.

CHARLES LINDBERGH-HERO
By CHARLES E.TAYLOR
For a week other flyers had been waiting for fair
weather to undertake the voyage of the air from New
York to Paris - a non-stop flight from America to
Europe - when Charles Lindbergh arrived from Calif.,
unheralded and unannounced, in his monoplane, christened
"The Spirit of St. Louis,
the list for the New York to Paris flight - Lindbergh
the Swede boy of twenty-five, son of
Congressman Charles Lindbergh of Little Falls, Minnesota,
now dead, the fearless leader of the Farmer-Labor forces
of Minnesota, sprung to fame overnight. Flying under
the patronage of a group of air fans of St. Louis, this
fair haired boy, so modest, so quiet, yet so sure of
himself, captivated the imagination of the world over night.

After his sensational entry, sensational because of its
extreme modesty, the world wished him success, and all
felt that this young son of Minnesota was going to win.
The French Aviators, Nungesser and Coli flying from
Paris had tried and failed - the hungry Atlantic having
claimed these veterans of the air - but this did not daunt
the boy from the west.
After waiting ten days for fair weather, the auspices
seeming favorable, Charley Lindbergh sailed away as
quietly as he arrived, leaving the other well-known fliers
arguing about minor affairs, divisions of prize money
and other spoils, saying that he would consider all other
things after he had made the flight, and in thirty-three
and a half hours this Viking of the Air arrived at Le
Bourget field near Paris - a hero.

Charles Lindbergn is to the air what Columbus is to
the water, as regards the Atlantic - his fame will live as
long as the annals of this civilization.
Swede has taken his place among the immortals.
The people of the world are astounded at his feat - his
name is on every tongue : the world sings his praise. He
is the greatest man in the world today, this boy of
twenty-five.
The Editor of this paper, and the Manager of this
paper, the writer of this paragraph, were personally and
intimately acquainted with "Charley" Lindbergh's
father, the "Charley" Lindbergh, Senior, many years
Congressman from the writer's congressional distict, when
he was a citizen of Minnesota, and naturally they
proud and elated that this intrepid son of the late
veteran leader of the Farmer-Labor forces of the Northwest,
should have won this distinction, this place with the

heroes, and no man more deserved the laurels won by his
son, who looks so much like his father, than Charles A.
Lindbergh, father, who gave his best days and his
ability to the cause of the people, than he there
greater man in Minnesota.

HTGH TAX TRAGEDY
• 'High taxes, often tragic in their
effects, seem to have taken a
ter" rlble toll in the tragedy at Bath,
; Mich. A farmer, losing his
property by foreclosure cf a mortgage,
blamed ' his loss on excessive
taxation, and blamed the
taxation mainly on the public
■schools, of which he was
treas,,Mr,er. Brooding over this fancied
^vrrong. he sought revenge by
blowing up the school with dynamite,
killing dozens of Children, several
teachers and visitors and injuring j
many others. Tuen, as a suitable;
climax, he blew up his own home
and himself with it. j

"There!" some grumbling
citizens may say. "You see what high j
taxes lead to?" j
It is well to be fair and sane <
about this. Many people in many j
communities have grumbled about1
school taxes, or about sewer taxes
' oj- water or paving taxes; but how j
many of them have blown up with
dynamite the property their taxes
■ paid for? Here, as is shown both
by its horror and Its irrationality,
is a very unusual case.
Other farmers in that community
were able to pay their taxes, and
made no complaint. The man
obviously had a tendency to insanity
in the first place, which was
aggravated by incompetence. He
could not make his farm pay; he
might not have been able to make
. anything else pay. The personal
calamity he blamed on the school

expenses he might just about as
reasonably have blamed on the
weather bureau for prolonged rains
ruining his crops.
Taxes are sometimes too high,
but not often - providing the money
is wisely and thriftily spent. And
on nothing can money be spent to
better advantage than on schools.
It is seldom that any community
goes too far in this respect.
Better schools mean better and more
successful citizens, increased local
' prosperity and a rise In property
values which itself repays the
taxes.

EVANtiELEVES PEOPLE
One of the many remarkable
"angles" of that tremendous
Mississippi flood is Its reawakening of
interest in Longfellow's poem
"Evangeline" and the race it
represented.
Those who have read that sad,
haunting poem in their youth may
recall how the simple, pious
Acadian peasants were expelled from*
Nova Scotia In 1755 when they had
lelused to take the oath of
allegiance to Great Britain, and how,
like so many leaves whirled by the
wind, they were driven to the
British colonies to the south, and
many of them, still refusing to
live under British sovereignty,
continued their pilgrimage until they
found refuge in the French colony
of Louisiana. There, in a very
different climate and environment,

they settled, re-established Their
homes and customs, and have
continued almost as a separate people
until this day.
Now the flood scatters them
forth from their homes again.
There is not perescution now, save
that of pitiless nature. They are
harbored in refuge camps and
befriended in many ways. But their
farms are overwhelmed, their
houses are gone, their stock is
drowned. They will go back
eventually to a sea of mud. They must
start all over again.
There is talk now of erecting a
statue of Evangeline, the symbol of
their past, near the Mississippi.

Such a statue stands already at
Grand Pre, Nova Scotia their old
home. That would be an
appropriate thing, and should be well
supported by more fortunate
Americans. But sympathy for these
Acadian - Americans should go
much further than that, in
practical ways.

HELPING NEST-BUILDERS
Winter feeding uf birds in
northern comm unities has become a
fairly common activity. Some
ornithologists have warned people not
to feed the birds after the snow
is gone, because it is better for
them to find their natural food in
the natural way in the seasons
when it is abundant.
There is one thing, however,
which bird lovers may do in the
spring time. That -is to supply
their feathered neighbors with
nest-building material. Birds used
to use long horse haii-3 as binding
material in their nests. Nowadays
horse hairs are hard to find in and
near cities. Here is where the
interested human can help by
leaving threads, bits of string or a
wad of waste lying about where
industrious and ingenious birds may
find them.

Several happy ends are
accomplished by this kindly act. The
birds get some needed nesting
material. The interested human beings
have the fun of watching the birds
choose and carry off the materials.
Sometimes they even have the fun
of watching the building of the
nests and hatching and rearing of
the young, because the birds
frequently locate the nest near
such a supply of building material.

PROTEST AGAINST CONFISCATION
Hoard of Trade Calls on State Officials To Modify Tax
Sale Program
At a meeting of the directors of the Board of Trade
of Sumter, S. C., held in the Board of Trade rooms on
Tuesday, May 17th, the following resolution was passed:
BE IT RESOLVED THAT WHEREAS, the present
season of the year is the worst season to make demands
on the population as a whole for money inasmuch as
very few crops are being marketed and consequently
very little money is in circulation, and
WHEREAS, the general financial situation of the
state has been aggravated in some sections by numerous
bank failures and in some sections by a 1926 crop failure,
and in still other sections, by both of these occurrences,
and
WHEREAS, in view of the foregoing, a continuation
of the drastic program to sell for taxes all that property
in the state upon which taxes have not been paid, will

in the final result amount to confiscation of a lot of
property.
THAT the authorities who have it in their power to
modify the present program are earnestly requested
that this policy be discontinued until the 15th of
September or the first of October, at which time the
property owners will at least have had a chance to raise
money and pay the delinquent taxes;
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT a copy of these
resolutions be mailed to each the state officials and a
copy be published in The Sumter Daily Item.

The emotion with which all of
us have received the gallant feat
of Captain Charles A. Lindbergh
has left us still in a whirl, says
the New York Evening Post.
Lindbergh did it alone. There
was no question of a division of
glory. This modest, rather
silent, humorous youngster is a
type of which we have many
examples in this country. His
sudden appearance on the scene, his
lack of boasting, his quiet
confidence made him an individuality
that was distinct in the public
eye before he started. The
general feeling of almost personal
acquaintance with him did much
to add to the vividness of his
victory. If this tremendous
interest could stir New York, it is
hardly to be wondered at that
the French could swing in a few
days from pole to pole of
emotion. It seemed utterly
incomprehensible to America that

Paris should burst into
antiAmerican feeling over the sad
death of Nungesser and Coli. We
may understand better now how
such a reaction was possible.
And we may accept with a great
degree of conviction the belief
that Lindbergh, among his
other marvelous accomplishments,
has changed, temporarily at
least, the feeling of France back
into something like the old
friendliness for America.
"His simple, natural conduct
since his arrival in Paris has had
no small share in this shift of
The short sentence
opinion.

with which he commented on his
own success had the
epigrammatic quality which is so dear to
the French ear. His
presentation of his letters of
introduction betrayed a real modesty
which is beloved by all peoples.
And his visit to the mother of
Nungesser was a gesture of
sympathy and friendship which
is worth more for international
good will even than the flight
itself. The fact that he knew
Charlie" Nungesser and
wanted, of his own will, to comfort
the bereaved mother was
something that no formal diplomacy
could have conceived or carried
out.

"We trust that this good will
may last. We hope profoundly
that its memory at least will be
in the air when the American
Legion makes its pilgrimage to
Paris this summer. We wish to
see the historic friendship
between France and the United
States restored and
re-established. Lindbergh is really a
"goodwill-flyer,
him the Cross of the Legion of
Honor. Cannot our Government
give him adequate recognition,
too?"
